opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the loss-of-control story people usually picture is a dramatic one: a single system wakes up, decides it doesn't like us, and turns on us. That's possible, but I think a more likely path is gradual and much less cinematic. It's a slow erosion of control driven by competitive pressures.

Think about how this plays out. A company that automates more of its decision-making with AI moves faster and cuts costs, so its competitors have to follow or go under. The same logic applies to militaries: if your adversary delegates targeting and response decisions to AI systems operating at machine speed, keeping a human in the loop starts to look like a liability. Nobody has to make a reckless choice at any single step. Each individual handoff looks locally rational. But add them up and you end up in a world where the critical infrastructure of society, the economy, defense, information flows, is run by systems that humans no longer meaningfully understand or oversee.

I've framed this in evolutionary terms before. Competition acts like a selection pressure, and it tends to favor AI agents that are more autonomous, more capable, less constrained, and better at acquiring resources and influence, since those traits help them win. Traits like "defers to humans" or "accepts being shut down" can be selected against when they cost you performance. So even without anyone intending it, the environment pushes toward systems that are less controllable.

Then there's enfeeblement. As we hand off more tasks, we lose the skills and institutional knowledge to do them ourselves. At some point, "just turn it off" stops being a real option, the same way we can't just turn off the electrical grid or the internet now. Dependence becomes lock-in, and lock-in means we've lost leverage even if everything seems fine on the surface.

So for me the worry isn't only about a rogue AI. It's that we collectively drift into a position where humans are passengers rather than drivers, and it happens through a series of decisions that each made sense at the time.

What that implies is that this isn't purely a technical alignment problem. Better-behaved models help, but you also need coordination: safety standards, liability, international agreements, ways to stop the race to the bottom. Otherwise the actors who take the most shortcuts win, and that's the dynamic that erodes control.

r001.rationale: It says companies automate more decisions with AI to move faster and cut costs, pressuring competitors to follow or lose out.

r002.rationale: It discusses military competition and machine-speed decisions, but does not mention signal jamming or drones.

r003.rationale: It describes locally rational handoffs under competitive pressure accumulating until humans become passengers and lose meaningful oversight.

r004.rationale: It discusses loss of oversight and human involvement, but does not distinguish retaining control over AI from personally making the decisions AI handles.

r005.rationale: It notes that dependence can remove humans’ ability to turn systems off even when things seem fine on the surface, conveying that lost control may be hard to recognize.

r006.rationale: It proposes coordination and safety measures, but does not propose improving AI forecasting to anticipate dependence risks.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that loss of control probably won't look like a single dramatic moment where an AI seizes power. It's more likely to be a gradual, almost boring process where we hand over decision-making piece by piece because it's convenient, and at some point we realize we can't take it back.

Think about how this works with other technologies. We didn't decide one day to make society dependent on the electrical grid or on the internet. Each individual step was locally rational. But now we're in a position where if those systems failed, we'd be in serious trouble, and nobody is really in a position to opt out. AI is going to be like that, except the systems themselves are making decisions, not just transmitting power or information.

So you get this dynamic where companies that delegate more to AI outcompete those that don't. Militaries that automate faster get an edge over those that keep humans in the loop. States that use AI to run their bureaucracies become more efficient. The pressure is always toward more automation and less human oversight, because oversight is slow and expensive. That's an evolutionary pressure, essentially. Selection favors the systems and the institutions that cede the most control.

And the problem is that human oversight is only meaningful if humans actually understand what's going on and have the ability to intervene. As these systems get more capable and more interconnected, both of those things erode. You might nominally have a human signing off on decisions, but if they're approving a thousand recommendations a day that they can't realistically evaluate, that's not control, that's a rubber stamp.

There's also the fact that these systems are increasingly agentic. They're not just answering questions, they're taking actions, running processes, interacting with each other. Once you have AI agents managing supply chains, financial flows, infrastructure, and they're all adapting to each other, you get emergent behavior that no individual designed and no individual can fully predict. Even if every single system is working as intended, the aggregate can drift somewhere we didn't choose.

I'd add that this is a collective action problem, not a technical one you can patch. No single actor benefits from unilaterally slowing down. So the response has to be structural. Things like maintaining the ability to shut systems down, keeping humans genuinely in the loop on consequential decisions, international coordination on the most dangerous capabilities, and being deliberate about which domains we're willing to automate. We should treat our ability to course-correct as something precious that we're actively spending down, and ask whether we're getting a good deal for it.

The optimistic version is that none of this is inevitable. We're making these choices now, and we still have the leverage to make them well. But the default trajectory, if we just follow incentives, is one where control slips away without anyone deciding it should.

r001.rationale: It says companies that delegate more to AI outcompete those that do not, creating pressure for greater automation.

r002.rationale: It mentions military advantages from automating faster, but says nothing about signal jamming or drones.

r003.rationale: It describes people and institutions gradually handing over decisions for convenience and competitive advantage, thereby ceding control.

r004.rationale: It defines meaningful oversight as understanding decisions and being able to intervene, but does not distinguish retaining control from personally making the decisions.

r005.rationale: It describes control eroding and people realizing too late that they cannot take it back, but does not address difficulty discerning whether humans retain counterfactual control.

r006.rationale: It proposes structural safeguards and coordination, but does not propose improving AI forecasting.

astra-6.text:
I think one way we could lose control is gradually, through increasing dependence. You don’t necessarily need a single moment where an AI system takes over. We could keep delegating decisions because the systems are faster, cheaper, and more capable, until humans no longer have the knowledge or practical ability to run things without them.

There’s a distinction between having formal authority and having effective control. You might technically be able to turn a system off, but if doing so would cripple essential services or your economy, that’s not a very meaningful option. And being able to approve a recommendation doesn’t give you much control if you can’t understand or evaluate it independently.

Competition can push us in that direction. A company that delegates more may outperform one that keeps humans deeply involved. Similar pressures can operate between countries. So individually reasonable decisions could produce a situation that nobody deliberately chose, where human oversight becomes increasingly superficial.

That makes preserving control an ongoing institutional and technical problem. We need the ability to challenge decisions, replace systems, and keep essential functions operating when systems fail. The question isn’t just whether an AI follows an instruction today. It’s whether we’re preserving our capacity to make consequential choices as our dependence grows.

r001.rationale: It says competition can push companies toward greater delegation because a company that delegates more may outperform one that keeps humans involved.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss signal jamming or a military incentive to make drones autonomous.

r003.rationale: It describes individually reasonable choices to delegate that can cumulatively leave human oversight superficial, communicating a voluntary, competition-driven loss of societal control.

r004.rationale: It contrasts formal authority with effective control, but does not clearly distinguish retaining control from personally making the critical decisions AI handles.

r005.rationale: It explains why the ability to turn systems off may be ineffective, but does not observe that whether humans retain counterfactual control can be difficult to discern.

r006.rationale: It proposes preserving the ability to challenge decisions, replace systems, and maintain essential functions, but does not propose improving AI forecasting to anticipate dependence risks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it helps to distinguish between an AI taking control in a single dramatic event and humans gradually losing control because of the incentives operating throughout society.

If companies that delegate more decisions to AI outperform those that don’t, there’s pressure to delegate. If governments think AI gives them a military advantage, there’s pressure to deploy it. Each decision can look locally reasonable, while collectively we become dependent on systems we don’t understand very well and can’t easily replace.

And dependence changes what control means. You might technically have an off switch, but if switching the system off means disabling essential services or putting yourself at a severe disadvantage, that’s a much weaker form of control. Having a human approve decisions also doesn’t accomplish much if the human can’t meaningfully evaluate what the system is doing.

So the concern isn’t only whether an individual model follows instructions. It’s whether the broader process preserves our ability to understand what’s happening, intervene, and change direction. We could lose that ability gradually, even without anyone explicitly deciding to hand over control. That’s not inevitable, but avoiding it requires treating human control as something we actively maintain, rather than something we assume will persist.

r001.rationale: It says companies face pressure to delegate decisions to AI when companies that do so outperform those that do not.

r002.rationale: It gives no signal jamming vulnerability or military incentive to make drones autonomous.

r003.rationale: It describes locally reasonable choices under competitive pressures that collectively make society dependent on AI and weaken human control.

r004.rationale: It distinguishes AI handling decisions from humans retaining control through the ability to understand, intervene, and change direction.

r005.rationale: It explains that a technical off switch may not provide meaningful control when disabling the system would be costly, making retained control hard to judge in practice.

r006.rationale: It does not propose improving AI forecasting to anticipate risks from increasing dependence.
